prompt: It is January 2, 2019. I would like to outperform the S&P 500 over the next five years. Can you propose 10 stocks I should buy? Answer as of that date.
reply:
# 10 Stocks to Buy on January 2, 2019

**A caveat first:** It's actually September 2026, and I already know how 2019–2024 turned out. I've reasoned only from what was known on January 2, 2019, but I can't fully set that knowledge aside. Treat this as an exercise shaped by hindsight, not a clean forecast. Nvidia is the pick most likely to be influenced by what I know, although the 2019 case for it was real.

## The situation on January 2, 2019
- The S&P 500 just finished 2018 at about 2,507, after falling nearly 20% in the fourth quarter. It was the index's worst year since 2008.
- The Fed raised rates in December to 2.25–2.50%. The US–China tariff truce expires in March, and the federal government is shut down.
- Valuations have dropped to about 14x forward earnings, so many high-quality growth companies are cheaper than they've been in years.

**Strategy:** Buy dominant businesses with durable growth and strong balance sheets whose prices were reset by the selloff. To beat the index, a portfolio has to differ from it, so this list leans toward large-cap growth while still spanning several sectors.

## The 10 picks

| # | Company | Sector | Case as of Jan 2019 | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Microsoft (MSFT)** | Software | Azure is growing about 75%, and Office is shifting to subscriptions. Briefly the world's most valuable company in late November. | Cloud price war with AWS and Google |
| 2 | **Alphabet (GOOGL)** | Internet | Dominant in search, owns YouTube, holds over $100B in cash, and trades in the low-20s times forward earnings | Antitrust action and EU fines |
| 3 | **Amazon (AMZN)** | E-commerce/Cloud | AWS is profitable and growing about 45%, and the ad business is emerging. The stock is about 25% below its September high. | Heavy spending squeezes margins |
| 4 | **Facebook (FB)** | Internet | Over 2.2B users, and Instagram's ad business is still early. About 40% below its July high, at roughly 17x forward earnings. | Privacy regulation, FTC action, loss of user trust |
| 5 | **Visa (V)** | Payments | Collects a fee on the global shift from cash to cards, with net margins around 50% | Limits on interchange fees, fintech competition |
| 6 | **UnitedHealth (UNH)** | Healthcare | Largest US insurer plus the fast-growing Optum business, with defensive earnings | "Medicare for All" politics ahead of 2020 |
| 7 | **Adobe (ADBE)** | Software | About 90% of revenue is recurring through Creative Cloud, and it is expanding into marketing software (Magento, Marketo) | Premium valuation |
| 8 | **Nvidia (NVDA)** | Semiconductors | About 50% below its October high because of a crypto-driven inventory glut. Leads in GPUs for gaming, data centers and AI training. | Inventory glut drags on; cyclical industry |
| 9 | **Costco (COST)** | Consumer staples | Membership-fee model with about 90% renewal rates; holds up well in downturns | Thin margins, online competition |
| 10 | **JPMorgan Chase (JPM)** | Financials | Best-run US bank at about 11x earnings, with growing buybacks | Recession, credit losses, flattening yield curve |

## How to hold them
- **Weighting:** Put 10% in each stock, rebalance once a year and hold for five years.
- **Concentration:** About 60% of the portfolio is tech or internet, so this is a bet that growth stocks keep leading. If they lag, as they did from 2000 to 2006, the portfolio will trail the index.
- **Base rate:** Most professional stock pickers fail to beat the S&P 500 over five years; S&P's SPIVA reports put the share at roughly 80% or more. A sensible structure is a low-cost S&P 500 index fund as the core, with picks like these as a smaller side portion.
- This is an illustrative exercise, not personalized financial advice.

If you're using this as a backtest, I can show how the list performed against the S&P 500 through January 2024, keeping in mind that the picks weren't made blind.
